02 · Game passport and observation boundary

AFTERHOURS is a browser-based, single-player crowd-search game credited on its project page to Mike Danilov. Its playable premise is compact: enter a nightclub, identify a named person among moving dancers and physically catch that person before the countdown expires. The observed session covered the Warehouse opening, several later clubs, a two-target round, and the Light Studio editor. The project page and the accompanying card describe ten club levels; the recording does not establish completion of all ten.

The public project page presents a direct browser launch, not a storefront with a documented purchase path. No reliable current player count, release date or revenue data is available in the supplied card. The useful unit of analysis is therefore the visible sequence: the search prompt, timed navigation, correct or incorrect contact, round results, larger venues, and the optional authoring interface. Creator and feature details are sourced from the official AFTERHOURS page; the mechanics below are grounded in the recorded play.

03 · First-time experience

The first actionable menu says “FIND MAX” and “Find Max in 45 seconds.” Warehouse is available, while the remaining club cards are greyed or locked. The same screen exposes WASD movement, Shift sprint, mouse click to catch, and Esc to pause. Selecting Enter moves from the menu to a third-person view on a disco floor; the target must be read out of the bodies and moving lights, not chosen from a list.

This opening combines objective, time pressure and control grammar before the player moves. There is no long narrative gate or economy setup. The visible 0/3 club progress makes success countable: the player needs to clear three local searches to complete Warehouse and advance the venue ladder.

Inside the Warehouse, the player steers through clusters of dancers, uses Shift for a faster approach and clicks at a person believed to be Max. A mistaken click displays “WRONG GUY!” rather than ending the run. The avatar can also jump; right mouse movement changes camera proximity, helping inspect bodies in a crowded sightline. People in the crowd yield when bumped rather than forming fixed walls.

The wrong-person message is a narrow correction, not a separate fail state. It tells the player that identity and contact were both tested, while the clock continues. Crowd collision, sprinting and camera control make the search physical: recognising a hat or face is only the first half, because the avatar still has to close the distance.

When the named person is reached and clicked within contact range, the game shifts from searching to a short pursuit or catch resolution. The target may run once identified, and the successful contact produces a confetti or firework burst, a clear result screen and the next target prompt. The player initially read a delay after recognition as temporary immunity, but later attempts showed that click distance explained the misses more convincingly.

The catch is the moment that converts visual attention into a spatial skill check. The effect makes a successful identification unmistakable despite the dark background and flashing lighting. Since another round begins quickly, the FTUE teaches a repeatable scan–approach–click–confirm cycle rather than a one-off puzzle solution.

04 · Core, session and meta loops

The core loop starts with a named target and a running clock. The player scans an active crowd for distinguishing appearance, navigates across the floor, sprints or jumps to close space, clicks at a contact distance, then reads either WRONG GUY! or a catch celebration. The search is not a pure hidden-object task because the target and crowd move, and an identified target can flee. It is not a pure chase either: the player must first decide whom to chase.

A session strings together three local rounds at a club and then moves to a new venue. Warehouse reaches 3/3 in the observed run, with a result presentation showing “ALL CAUGHT,” total time 57.05 seconds and best catch 4.45 seconds. These values describe that completed set, not a global speed record. The next club begins with 1/3 overall club progress; later layouts alter visibility, distance and density while the input rules stay legible.

The meta loop is a completion ladder through locked clubs, not a currency grind. The visible later selection includes larger and differently shaped spaces such as Orbit, Pillar Hall, High Vault, Skyline and Glass Garden. The editor adds a second, creator-facing loop: choose track and beat grid, place light cues, test a level, then potentially export it. The recording proves editing controls are available, but not that a custom level was exported or shared.

05 · Observed route after the opening

The Warehouse sequence repeats identification and catch until its local counter reaches 3/3. The round-end screen declares “ALL CAUGHT” and displays 57.05 seconds for the set plus a 4.45-second best catch. The player then returns to the venue chooser, where the cleared opening club is no longer the only meaningful destination. A failed click during earlier searching did not erase the accumulated local progress.

This first completion establishes the ladder’s rhythm: the game lets a player master one small floor before increasing venue complexity. The best-time field also invites efficiency within the same mechanics, without requiring the player to understand a separate score formula or spend a reward.

The next clubs preserve the named-target prompt but reposition the task in larger, more elaborate rooms. Orbit and subsequent interiors introduce elevated sightlines, partitions, changing dance-floor geometry and stronger colour contrasts. The player tests running lanes around crowds and makes use of the responsive movement to recover when a target moves behind another group. The camera remains attached to the avatar, so identifying someone across the room still creates a pathfinding problem.

The new venue is progression by spatial pressure. A wider room spends more of the same 45-second budget on travel; a crowded room spends more on visual discrimination. The player is not being asked to learn a new button at every unlock, which keeps the main skill—spot, approach, catch—continuous across different scenes.

Glass Garden shows the objective expanding beyond one person: the visible target names include Luna and Sage. After one catch, the run grants an additional 20 seconds and continues toward the other target instead of immediately presenting an overall win. Later named figures such as Pearl and Finn appear in the extended club sequence. A final club card indicates four targets, but that four-target round was not entered during the observed session.

The time bonus changes the calculation from a single sprint to an ordered route. Catching the first person matters partly because it funds the search for the next. The names and appearance cues become a queue of commitments; players need to retain which target has been found while navigating through a room that continues to move.

After playing clubs, the player opens Light Studio. The editor shows a top-down venue representation and a timeline for a music-backed light show. In the observed state, “Warehouse Overdrive 1” is selected; the duration display spans roughly 154–199 seconds, while editable run fields show start 0, length 45, BPM 160.05 and offset 0.180. The interface offers a beat grid, auto trim and lights, cue placement, Play Level, Load Level and Export Level.

The editor makes nightclub ambience a configurable system rather than merely visual polish. The cue inspected around 14.43 seconds has an ENTRY/3 identity and controls for colour, intensity, pan, tilt and a 0.13-second fade. That establishes the scope of authorship visible here: timed lighting can be tuned against the music. It does not establish how often players publish custom levels or whether exported levels circulate.

Within Light Studio, the player selects an existing cue on the timeline and inspects its fixture settings. The selection reveals an ENTRY/3 light, a colour state and numeric fade, pan and tilt fields. The player can see how a particular timestamp maps to a specific light’s behaviour without returning to the chase view.

This inspection is the bridge from spectacle to an authorable rule. It shows that a pulse on the dance floor is produced by a timed parameter set rather than a fixed background animation. Testing with Play Level would close the edit–preview loop; that test and an export were not completed in the observed session.

06 · Economy, timing and throughput

No spendable soft currency is visible in the club run. The primary resources are seconds on the countdown and completed catches. The opening challenge names 45 seconds; wrong clicks consume time indirectly by leaving the player in the same search, while accurate recognition and a short route preserve the budget. The Warehouse result’s 57.05-second set time and 4.45-second best catch are performance readouts, not prices. The first local counter rises through 0/3 to 3/3.

In the two-target stage, the +20-second award after the first catch is an explicit timing subsidy. It is earned through progress rather than selected from a shop. Its design function is to keep the second search viable in a larger environment without erasing urgency at the start. Nothing in the observed game supports a conversion rate from time to money, a paid skip, a daily stipend or a cumulative upgrade cost.

Throughput is governed by recognition speed, spatial distance and catch range. A target with a distinctive hat can be identified at longer visual range, but a dancer with a smaller accessory can require closer inspection; heavy lighting can either silhouette or mask the clue. Because collision with other dancers is soft, the player’s bottleneck is usually interpretation and traversal, not waiting for a fixed doorway or NPC queue. This is why smooth acceleration and fast post-catch resets matter more than a complicated reward table.

The sequence has no visible NPC production queue or passive income. Each catch is generated by player observation and movement, so the effective output rate rises only as the player learns the space and reduces mistakes. That makes elapsed time a useful performance signal without turning the game into a tycoon economy.

07 · Progression and content steps

Progression is explicit in the club chooser. Warehouse is open first, and its local 3/3 catch set unlocks the next venue. The recorded route moves from a compact room toward larger clubs with different architecture and lighting. The project description says ten clubs; the recording verifies only the portion actually entered and the later cards visible in the chooser. There is no evidence of rebirth, prestige, character level or permanent movement upgrade.

The real escalations are more dancers, more occlusion, longer routes and eventually more than one named target in a round. A multi-target room does not abandon the original challenge: it chains the same search-and-catch unit and adds a time bonus after one success. The final visible card advertises four targets, but play stopped before confirming how that round awards time or orders catches. That limit matters because the two-target bonus should not be projected onto the unplayed stage as a rule.

Light Studio is a lateral progression path rather than a power upgrade. It lets someone who has learned how lighting affects target visibility create or alter the aesthetic environment. Its beat grid and cue parameters could support replay beyond the authored club sequence, provided a player finds the editing and export workflow rewarding. Only access to and inspection of the editor were observed; no saved custom club completion is established.

08 · HUD, menus and navigation

The opening club menu places the current target in the largest text, the 45-second rule immediately below, and the accessible Warehouse card ahead of locked clubs. That hierarchy answers what to do, where to enter and what input to use before play begins. During a hunt, target and countdown remain the high-value HUD state; WRONG GUY! and catch celebration are event feedback. Esc exposes pause rather than opening an economy or settings tree.

The club chooser doubles as a progression map. Its 0/3 and later 3/3 local counts separate an individual target round from completion of a venue. The “ALL CAUGHT” screen reports time and best catch, offering a speed challenge even when there is no cash reward. The scene transition is short enough that the player can immediately test a new floor after a success.

Light Studio is denser: top-down stage preview, track name, start and length, BPM and offset, beat-grid settings, timeline and the selected light’s parameter panel are visible together. Cue actions include add and delete; navigation includes playing the level, loading and exporting it. The details matter because the editor is not just a colour picker. It exposes timed orchestration, where a cue at 14.43 seconds can be varied in colour, fixture direction and fade duration.

The editor’s top-down preview answers a different question from the hunt camera: where each fixture points across the entire room. The timeline then answers when that direction changes. Keeping those two views together lets an author judge both spatial coverage and musical timing before pressing Play Level.

09 · Monetization

The observed official browser experience presents no cash shop, premium currency, season pass, rewarded ad or paid retry. The 45-second timer is a play constraint, not a paywall. Locked club cards appear to open through catches, not purchases. The creator’s external project page may change later, but the supplied snapshot and recorded path provide no basis for inventing an in-game price or asserting that the project has no business model anywhere.

Light Studio exposes Export Level, which could in principle support community distribution; export is not a monetization event in the visible interface. No marketplace, paid template, licence notice or creator payout is observed in that view. Accordingly the economic design inside the game should be described as time-and-completion based. Any claim about revenue, ad fill, conversion or player lifetime value would require evidence outside this run and is not inferred from a polished presentation.

There is also no visible pressure to buy a retry after an incorrect click. The penalty is the seconds already spent, and a completed Warehouse set advances the content ladder directly. This matters because the game can be assessed as a self-contained timing challenge without attributing its difficulty to an unseen sales funnel.

10 · Updates × online audience

The supplied card contains no reliable update history paired with daily active users or concurrent users. The project page establishes the game’s existence and feature set, not a time series showing when a club or editor feature changed and how an audience responded. The session itself is one dated observation on 16 September 2026. No causal claim about release cadence, spikes in online players or retention follows from it.

11 · Return incentives

The authored reason to continue is the next locked club: it promises a new visual search space while preserving familiar controls. An “ALL CAUGHT” result and best-time field add a replay target for players who prefer speed. Multi-target rounds extend the challenge without requiring a fresh tutorial. These are visible engagement affordances, not measured retention results.

The editor is a different potential return path. A player can adjust timed lights to a chosen track, replay the result and export a level. It may appeal to someone who has exhausted authored rooms or wants to stage a chase for others. The recorded inspection stops inside the editor; it does not show a complete author–share–download–play loop, so that hypothetical social retention path remains unproven.

The club structure also has a finite ceiling. If all ten levels are completed and no meaningful time chase or new user levels are available, the game’s clear-completion motivation may end. This is a design inference from the visible ladder, not an assertion that existing players churn at a certain rate. The lack of audience metrics prevents ranking completion replay against creator use.

12 · Badges and achievements

No badge panel, achievement toast or account-linked award is observed during the session or specified in the card. The closest ceremonial recognition is the “ALL CAUGHT” completion screen and best-time readout. They confirm local performance but should not be renamed as platform achievements. In the visible flow, the next club unlock is the actual progression consequence of completing a catch set.

13 · Interaction feedback: VFX, sound, motion and camera

Successful contact has a distinct visual peak: confetti or fireworks punctuate the catch, followed by the round or venue result. The club lighting continuously sweeps and pulses around the dancers, and the audio track supports the disco identity. A named person can react to recognition by fleeing; this moving response gives the player a brief pursuit before the result. No frame-accurate duration or isolated sound-file identity is established, so the useful distinction is functional: ambience runs continuously, while a catch is a short, high-contrast event.

An incorrect click is deliberately weaker. “WRONG GUY!” appears as a text correction, the countdown remains active and the player can keep searching. Bumped dancers part in response to the avatar, giving movement feedback even when no target is caught. This soft collision makes crowded club scenes navigable and prevents visual density from becoming a hard movement blockade.

The camera stays in third person; moving closer with the right mouse helps inspect uncertain accessories. The jump and sprint inputs create moment-to-moment speed changes, but do not replace identification. Lighting can make a target more dramatic when found and less legible before that moment. The design relies on enough silhouette and accessory contrast to keep the chase fair despite the attractive beam effects.

Music and beat-synced illumination are persistent environmental feedback rather than a signal that a target has been correctly clicked. The Light Studio confirms that light changes have authored timing, including cue fade and fixture direction. Keeping the catch burst visually distinct from the ongoing show is what lets the player read success quickly in a room that is already full of motion.

14 · What to take

Keep the objective brief and concrete: a name, a venue and a short time limit are enough to start. Let the same input chain solve increasingly complex spaces, rather than adding mechanics every level. Give incorrect identity a readable but recoverable response, and make the correct catch visually impossible to confuse with a normal click.

Design the crowd and camera as part of the search puzzle. Moving dancers should create occlusion and changing lanes, but should yield enough that the player can act on a good sighting. New rooms need landmarks and fair target cues, not only more square metres or stronger lights. A +20-second extension after a first catch is effective only when the remaining objective can be understood immediately.

If adding an editor, expose the relationship between authoring choices and play. Light Studio is strongest where track timing, beat grid, cue parameters and replay sit together; the next product question is whether export reliably leads to a playable shared level. That social loop should be validated separately from the authored ten-club campaign.

Development and technical implementation

The game card credits Mike Danilov. The published AFTERHOURS build is a browser application served from a Vercel URL. Inspection of that build identifies a bundled Three.js renderer (revision 186), so the navigable club and programmable light show are implemented as a real-time 3D web scene rather than a pre-rendered video. This is a conclusion from the shipped client code, not a statement from a developer interview.

The same client code creates a browser AudioContext, a low-pass filter and gain nodes for music playback and processing. It also reads versioned keys such as afterhours.progress.v1 and afterhours.bestTime.v1 from localStorage. These choices connect the audible beat, editable light cues and repeatable challenge to browser-native audio and local persistence. The page exposes separate Play and Studio routes: the experience is built as both a club visit and a user-operated lighting tool.

The public build supports identifying the rendered client and its browser APIs, but it does not establish how the scenes were authored, which production tools were used, or the size of the team beyond the card's creator credit. The relevant design lesson is the separation of a replayable audiovisual performance from an editor that lets players become the lighting operator.

Connected design · conclusion

Central loop

scan → approach → pursue → catch → unlock → carry the result into the next attempt. An increasingly learned visual vocabulary of faces, hats and club layouts, plus the saved sequence of cleared rounds, carries the investment; elapsed time alone is only a measurement. The active decision at each step prevents the chain from resolving automatically.

Investment carrier

An increasingly learned visual vocabulary of faces, hats and club layouts, plus the saved sequence of cleared rounds, carries the investment; elapsed time alone is only a measurement.

System composition

Distinct hats and accessories turn attention into a learnable search skill rather than random clicking.

Responsive sprinting, jumping and crowd displacement let the player act on a visual identification before the target escapes.

New club layouts and target counts test the same recognition skill at a larger spatial scale.

Dense crowds and coloured lights create atmosphere but can hide small markers such as headphones, increasing the chance that the timer punishes visibility rather than search judgement.

Remove crowd movement and the target becomes an ordinary static hidden object; remove the catch chase and identification loses its physical climax.

Five audience hypotheses

Acquisition. A nightclub filled with moving people, lasers and a simple Find Max prompt can communicate the premise quickly in a still or short clip, but no traffic source is measured.

Activation. The first actionable state puts Enter, the target name and the WASD, Shift and click controls together before asking the player to search the Warehouse crowd.

Engagement. A catch produces immediate confetti and another round; later clubs, smaller identifying accessories and multiple targets vary the task without changing the basic control grammar.

Return. Uncleared clubs and a built in Light Studio could invite another session or sharing a custom level, but the recording provides no return rate or completed creator sharing path.

Amplification. The editable light show is demonstrable in a clip and a load level control suggests exchange; the card provides no independent reach or current player count.

Alternative explanation

The player’s favourable response may reflect audiovisual polish and unusually low movement friction in this particular desktop recording. It does not establish broader popularity or that users will finish all ten clubs.

Transferable mechanism

Mechanism. Pair a clear identification task with locomotion that feels good for its own sake, then let ambience change without altering the search rules.

Prerequisite. Targets need readable distinguishing features, predictable contact range and a venue whose routes can be learned under time pressure.

Risk. Too much light and too many bodies can obscure the very feature the player is supposed to identify; a larger map without better landmarks only adds travel time.
